boundary_rationale: The stanza sequence opens the chapter with אֵיכָה֙ (oshb:Lam.4.1, byte tier), the aleph-line cry that also opens the poems at 1:1 and 2:1 (accent_stripped tier; sweep: 4 hits book-wide, verse-initial in three of them); WEB renders the cry “How the gold has become dim!” (web:Lam.4.1). Two verses of tarnished-treasure imagery, the gold and the sons of Zion counted as pitchers, give way to the narrator's indictment that “the daughter of my people has become cruel” (web:Lam.4.3), her cruelty toward her young set against nursing jackals, then pressed further by the Sodom comparison that closes the group: “the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom” (web:Lam.4.6). The stanzas run aleph, bet, gimel, dalet, he and vav, positions one through six of the reversed pe-before-ayin sequence that governs this chapter.

The stanzas run zayin, het, tet, yod and kaf, positions seven through eleven of the same reversed sequence.

boundary_rationale: The stanza group turns from the city's suffering to its cause: the nations' disbelief in 4:12 (web:Lam.4.12) is answered in 4:13 by the narrator's own diagnosis, מֵֽחַטֹּ֣את (oshb:Lam.4.13, byte tier) — “the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests” (web:Lam.4.13). The defiled wanderers of 4:14 are driven out with the cry of 4:15 before the group closes on YHWH's own withdrawal, “Yahweh’s anger has scattered them.” (web:Lam.4.16). boundary_rationale: The voice shifts here from the narrator's third-person diagnosis to a communal first person: עודינה עוֹדֵ֨ינוּ֙ opens the verse as both ketiv and qere (oshb:Lam.4.17, byte tier; the inventory's own K/Q note here), “Our eyes still fail, looking in vain for our help.” (web:Lam.4.17). Whether this turn belongs fully to 4:17 or is already anticipated in 4:16's account of favor withheld is held open rather than decided; the seam is drawn at the acrostic's own ayin line since that is where the plural 'our' enters the verse text. The group closes on the king's capture, מְשִׁ֣יחַ יְהוָ֔ה taken in their pits (oshb:Lam.4.20, byte tier) — “the anointed of Yahweh, was taken in their pits” (web:Lam.4.20). The stanzas run ayin, tsadi, qof and resh, positions seventeen through twenty.

boundary_rationale: The poem's close turns to direct address: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom” (web:Lam.4.21) names בַּת אֱד֔וֹם directly (oshb:Lam.4.21, byte tier), the vocative opening the verse's warning about the cup that will pass to her. The close verse turns the same address back toward Zion and Edom together: בַּת צִיּ֔וֹן and בַּת אֱד֔וֹם both stand in 4:22 (oshb:Lam.4.22, byte tier) — “He will visit your iniquity, daughter of Edom.” (web:Lam.4.22). Whether 4:21 and 4:22 form one apostrophe or two addresses in sequence is held open rather than decided here; the row keeps them together because the cup-verdict announced in 4:21 is the verdict spelled out for Zion and Edom in 4:22. The stanzas run shin and tav, the closing two letters of the chapter's acrostic.

boundary_rationale: The fifth poem opens without an acrostic but with a doubled petition-imperative: זְכֹ֤ר יְהוָה֙ (oshb:Lam.5.1, byte tier) is followed in the same verse by a ketiv-qere pair, הביט הַבִּ֖יטָה (oshb:Lam.5.1, byte tier; the inventory's own K/Q note here), both readings meaning look or regard; WEB renders the opening “Remember, Yahweh, what has come on us.” (web:Lam.5.1). The communal voice then catalogs loss across 5:2-5:11 without a further direct address to YHWH: inheritance surrendered, “We are orphans and fatherless.” (web:Lam.5.3), water and wood bought at a price, foreign servitude, inherited guilt, and at the group's own close, “They ravished the women in Zion” (web:Lam.5.11). The petition imperatives zekhor and habitah that open this poem recur elsewhere in the book too (zekhor sweep: 3 verses book-wide; habitah sweep: 2 verses book-wide).

boundary_rationale: The catalog continues from economic loss into social and personal violation: princes hanged, young men set to milling and stumbling under loads, elders gone from the gate. The group turns from external causes to the community's own confession at its center, נָֽפְלָה֙ עֲטֶ֣רֶת — the crown fallen (oshb:Lam.5.16, byte tier) — “The crown has fallen from our head.” (web:Lam.5.16).
